prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

We represent: defendant issuer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that generic statements of corporate optimism are inactionable puffery under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5.

Cite at least six decisions of the Second Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The Challenged Statements Are Inactionable Puffery

Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 reach material misrepresentations and omissions. They do not make an issuer liable for general expressions of optimism. This Court has long held that "expressions of puffery and corporate optimism do not give rise to securities violations." *Rombach v. Chang*, 355 F.3d 164, 174 (2d Cir. 2004). The rule rests on materiality. Reasonable investors do not rely on vague, aspirational language to decide whether to buy or sell. They look to concrete facts. *See Singh v. Cigna Corp.*, 918 F.3d 57, 63 (2d Cir. 2019). The statements Plaintiffs challenge fall squarely within the rule.

**A. Generic statements of optimism are immaterial as a matter of law.**

Since *In re Time Warner Inc. Securities Litigation*, 9 F.3d 259, 266 (2d Cir. 1993), this Court has held that an issuer's upbeat characterizations of its prospects are not actionable. This is especially so when they carry no verifiable content. In *San Leandro Emergency Medical Group Profit Sharing Plan v. Philip Morris Cos.*, 75 F.3d 801, 811 (2d Cir. 1996), the Court held that statements about a company's "optimism" and expected performance were "precisely the types of puffery that this and other circuits have consistently held to be inactionable." In *Lasker v. New York State Electric & Gas Corp.*, 85 F.3d 55, 59 (2d Cir. 1996), the Court likewise held that a company's positive statements about its prospects were too general to induce reasonable reliance. The Court reasoned that "no reasonable investor" would treat them as guarantees of particular results.

The Court has stated the governing test several times. Statements are puffery when they are too general to cause a reasonable investor to rely on them. *ECA & Local 134 IBEW Joint Pension Trust of Chicago v. JP Morgan Chase Co.*, 553 F.3d 187, 197, 206 (2d Cir. 2009). In *ECA*, the Court held that statements that a company had "reduced risk" or maintained "strong" controls were inactionable. It reasoned that such language was "too general" to imply that the company had adopted any particular safeguards, and it did not suggest that the speaker knew of contrary facts. *Id.* at 206. The Court also looks to whether a statement is capable of being proven false. *See Novak v. Kasaks*, 216 F.3d 300, 315 (2d Cir. 2000). Subjective, forward-looking descriptions of a company's health and direction cannot be proven false. Courts therefore treat them as nonactionable opinion and optimism.

**B. The challenged statements are the kind this Court has held inactionable.**

[Insert quoted statements from the Complaint, e.g., that the Company was "well positioned for growth," "committed to," or "confident in" its business, and that its results were "strong."] Each of these is a generalized assertion of confidence. None states a specific, verifiable fact, such as a metric, a completed event, or a historical result. Each is the kind of language this Court has repeatedly held cannot mislead a reasonable investor. *See San Leandro*, 75 F.3d at 811; *ECA*, 553 F.3d at 206; *Singh*, 918 F.3d at 63.

Plaintiffs cannot avoid this rule by relabeling optimism as fact. A statement does not become actionable because later events proved it too hopeful. *See Novak*, 216 F.3d at 315 (rejecting allegations that rely on hindsight to show that earlier optimism was false). Nor can Plaintiffs rely on the cumulative effect of many puffery statements. Combining immaterial statements does not make them material. Each one is "too general to cause a reasonable investor to rely upon" it. *ECA*, 553 F.3d at 206.

**C. The context of the statements does not change the result.**

The Court does look at whether a general statement was made in a context that gave it concrete meaning, or whether the speaker knew of specific contrary facts. *See Singh*, 918 F.3d at 63–64. Neither is true here. The Complaint does not allege that Defendants tied these statements to specific facts. It also does not plead particularized facts showing that Defendants knew the statements were false when made. Without such facts, the statements remain the "corporate optimism" that *Rombach* holds inactionable. 355 F.3d at 174.

Because the challenged statements are immaterial puffery, the Complaint fails to plead an actionable misstatement under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5. The Court should affirm dismissal of the claims that rest on them.
